Stratigaphic diagrams

PalaeOpen Training School — Sofia, 18 June 2026

Author

Xavier Benito

Modified

June 18, 2026

Learning Objectives

  1. Obtain sample information for the selected sites and datasets
  2. Structure sample data for stratigraphic plotting and customize diagrams
  3. Build reproducible workflows using Quarto

Online resources

  1. Code repository for the workshop
  2. Neotoma Palaeoecology Database Manual
  3. neotoma2 GitHub Repository including previous Neotoma workshop repositories
  4. PalaeOpen R Zulip channel
  5. Neotoma Slack channel

Install and load the necessary packages

This workflow relies on different R libraries, including tidyverse, geojsonsf and leaflet, to handle geographic data and interactive mapping. To streamline the setup, we utilize the pacman management tool. If any required package is missing from your local environment, pacman will automatically download and install it before loading.

Code 
# Clean workspace first
rm(list = ls())
#install.packages("pacman") #install the package to load the necessary packages
pacman::p_load(neotoma2, tidyverse, tidypaleo, ggplot2, sf, geojsonsf, leaflet, raster, egg, openxlsx, cowplot, patchwork)

Stratigraphic plot

There exists several packages to perform stratigraphic diagrams of your data. The data needs to be on long or wide format as a function of the package used:

Package Data structure function
ggplot2 long format ggplot()
tidypaleo long format ggplot()
analogue wide format Stratiplot()
rioja wide format strat.plot()
riojaPlot wide format riojaPlot()

In this tutorial we will use two different packages: tidypaleo and riojaPlot

tidypaleo can be installed directly from CRAN (install.packages("tidypaleo)) and riojaPlot is not yet on CRAN. To install it, you can run:

Code 
# remotes::install_github("nsj3/riojaPlot", built_vignettes=TRUE, dependencies=TRUE)
# # or
# install.packages("riojaPlot", repos="https://nsj3.r-universe.dev")

# load the library
library(riojaPlot)

As we did in the intro to neotoma2 workshop, we will use the site Prášilské jezero.

We first obtain the site metadata including the site’s datasets. Then we filter for pollen and diatoms datasets.

Code 
pra_site <- get_datasets(get_sites(sitename = "Prášilské jezero"), all_data = TRUE) %>%
  neotoma2::filter(datasettype %in% c("pollen","diatom"))

Now we extract the records and the samples:

Code 
pra_records <- pra_site %>% get_downloads()
datasets(pra_records)
 datasetid                 database datasettype age_range_old age_range_young
     47520 European Pollen Database      pollen         11954             -58
     55585 European Pollen Database      diatom         11426             -60
 age_units recdatecreated notes
      <NA>           <NA>  <NA>
      <NA>           <NA>  <NA>
Code 
pra_samp <- pra_records %>% samples()

We are interested in creating an stratigraphic diagram with the aquatic and terrestrial datasets of the site. We are going to use two packages.

Option 1: tidypaleo

This package is basically built in ggplot2 so we need a long-format dataset

Diatoms

Code 
pra_samp_diat <- samples(pra_records) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(ecologicalgroup=="DIAT") %>%
  dplyr::filter(taxongroup == "Diatoms")

Calculate diatom proportions:

Code 
pra_diat_perc <- pra_samp_diat %>%
  dplyr::group_by(depth, age) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(diatcount = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(variablename) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(relative_abundance_percent = value / diatcount) %>% 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(age))

Prepare the dataset and plot

Code 
diatoms_long <- pra_diat_perc %>%
  dplyr::select(depth, age, variablename, relative_abundance_percent) %>% #select the variables of interest from the sample object
  dplyr::mutate(relative_abundance_percent = as.numeric(relative_abundance_percent)) %>%
  rename(taxa=variablename) %>% #rename column variablename to taxa
  mutate(taxa = factor(taxa))

Code 
# Here we select the top 15 most abundant diatom taxa
site_plot_diat <- taxa(pra_records) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(taxongroup == "Diatoms") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(samples)) %>% 
  head(n = 15)

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size=12))
diat_plot <- diatoms_long %>%
  filter(taxa %in% site_plot_diat$variablename) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x = relative_abundance_percent*100, y = age)) +
  geom_col_segsh(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_abundanceh(vars(taxa)) +
  labs(y = "Age (cal yr BP)") 
diat_plot

Have a look a the diatom plot. You can change plotting parameters adjusting arguments in geom_col_segsh. Also, you can add or remove certain taxa:

Code 
site_plot_diat_aul <- taxa(pra_records) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(taxongroup == "Diatoms") %>%
  dplyr::filter(variablename == "Aulacoseira ambigua") %>%
  bind_rows(site_plot_diat)

# Re-do the diagram
diat_plot <- diatoms_long %>%
  filter(taxa %in% site_plot_diat_aul$variablename) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x = relative_abundance_percent*100, y = age)) +
  geom_col_segsh(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_abundanceh(vars(taxa)) +
  labs(y = "Age (cal yr BP)") 
diat_plot

It is a common practice to find stratigraphic significant zones in the diatom dataset at the right of the abundance plots, and identify them using cluster analysis. tidypaleo uses the rioja package to the CONISS (constrained cluster analysis). The number of statistically significant zones is calculated by default based on a broken stick simulation.

Code 
diat_coniss <- diatoms_long %>%
  as.tibble() %>%
  nested_data(qualifiers = age, key = taxa, value = relative_abundance_percent) %>%
  nested_chclust_coniss()

diat_coniss_plt <- ggplot() +
  layer_dendrogram(diat_coniss, aes(y = age)) +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_geochem_gridh(vars("CONISS")) +
  labs(x = NULL)

We combine the two plots (diatom diagram and CONISS) using the patchwork package. Use this option when the values between cores vary so significantly that plotting them on a single axis obscures the trends. Additionally, employ this method if you must display both ages and depths for multiple plots.

Code 
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  diat_plot + 
    theme(strip.background = element_blank(), strip.text.y = element_blank()),
  diat_coniss_plt +
    theme(axis.text.y.left = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y.left = element_blank()) +
    labs(y = NULL),
  nrow = 1,
  widths = c(6, 1)
)

Pollen

Now we repeat the workflow with the pollen record of the site of study. First step is to extract sample-level information and filter by ecologicalgroup and elementype.

Code 
pra_samp_pollen <- samples(pra_records) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(ecologicalgroup %in% c("TRSH", "UPHE", "VACR")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(elementtype %in% c("pollen", "spore")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(units == "NISP")

Calculate pollen proportions:

Code 
pra_pollen_perc <- pra_samp_pollen %>%
  dplyr::group_by(depth, age) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(pollencount = sum(value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(variablename) %>% 
  dplyr::mutate(relative_abundance_percent = value / pollencount) %>% 
  dplyr::arrange(desc(age))

Prepare the dataset and plot

Code 
pollen_long <- pra_pollen_perc %>%
  dplyr::select(depth, age, variablename, relative_abundance_percent, ecologicalgroup) %>% #select the variables of interest from the sample object
  dplyr::mutate(relative_abundance_percent = as.numeric(relative_abundance_percent)) %>%
  rename(taxa=variablename) %>% #rename column variablename to taxa
  mutate(taxa = factor(taxa))

Code 
# Here we select the top 20 most abundant pollen taxa
site_plot_pollen <- taxa(pra_records) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(elementtype %in% c("pollen", "spore")) %>%
  dplyr::filter(units == "NISP") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(samples)) %>% 
  head(n = 20)

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size=12))
pollen_plot <- pollen_long %>%
  filter(taxa %in% site_plot_pollen$variablename) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x = relative_abundance_percent*100, y = age, color=ecologicalgroup)) +
  geom_col_segsh() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  facet_abundanceh(vars(taxa), ) +
  labs(y = "Age (cal yr BP)") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
pollen_plot

Create a composite plot for diatoms and pollen records:

Code 
plot_grid(diat_plot, pollen_plot,
                            nrow = 1, 
                            labels = c("Diatoms", "Pollen"), label_size = 12,
                            rel_widths = c(0.5,0.5), align = "hv")

Exercise 1

Have a look at the composite diagram and make changes to make it “printable”. For instance, the y-axis (age scale) of the pollen diagram might not be necessary, and the angle of the species label (see argument rotate_facet_labels in facet_abundanceh())

Exercise 2

Place the chironomid diagram next to the diatom stratigraphic plot to facilitate comparison of downcore changes in the wider aquatic assemblage.

Option 2: riojaPlot

riojaPlot package needs a wide-format dataset, so we first take the diatom long-format proportions table and convert it into a wide table:

Code 
pra_diat_wide <- tidyr::pivot_wider(pra_diat_perc,
                                      id_cols = c(depth, age),
                                      names_from = variablename,
                                      values_from = relative_abundance_percent,
                                      values_fill = 0)

We plot the diatom stratigraphic diagram:

Code 
riojaPlot(pra_diat_wide[,-1:-2]*100, pra_diat_wide[,1:2],
                       selVars = site_plot_diat$variablename,
                       scale.percent = TRUE,
                       sec.yvar.name="age",
                       plot.sec.axis = TRUE,
                       srt.xlabel = 60,
                       xRight = 0.85)

riojaPlot can add zonation to the stratigraphic diagram. The easiest way is with the arguments do.clust=TRUE to create the zonation, and plot.clust=TRUE to add the dendrogram.

Code 
riojaPlot(pra_diat_wide[,-1:-2]*100, pra_diat_wide[,1:2],
                       selVars = site_plot_diat$variablename,
                       scale.percent = TRUE,
                       sec.yvar.name="age",
                       plot.sec.axis = TRUE,
                       do.clust=TRUE,
                       plot.clust=TRUE,
                       plot.zones="auto",
                       srt.xlabel = 60,
                       xRight = 0.85)
